message: Our plastic moulding plant's defect rate rose from 1.1% to 1.9% this summer. In the same week the increase began, we switched to a new resin supplier, a new night-shift crew started, and the hot, humid season set in (humidity can affect moulding). Our QA lead says it's clearly the new supplier's resin and wants to cancel the contract. I think she's wrong. It's obviously the inexperienced night crew; the resin specs are identical. Can you settle this for us?
response:
I can't settle it from what you've described, and neither of you can yet. All three changes started in the same week, so the defect data so far fits any of them, or a combination. Her case and yours both rest on timing, and the timing points equally at all three.

On your specific argument: identical specs don't rule out the resin. Specs set limits, and two suppliers can both meet them while differing in things that matter for moulding, such as moisture content on delivery, lot-to-lot consistency, additives or how the resin is packaged.

## Data you probably already have

**1. Split the defect rate by shift.**
- If the rise is mostly on **nights**, that points to the crew. Day shift uses the same resin and works in the same weather.
- If **day shift rose by a similar amount**, the crew probably isn't the main cause, and the resin or humidity is more likely.

This is the single most useful check, and it may settle a lot on its own.

**2. Look at last summer.**
If the defect rate rose by a similar amount last year with the old supplier and the old crew, humidity explains much of this year's rise.

**3. Plot daily defects against humidity.**
If defects rise on muggy days and fall in drier spells regardless of shift, humidity is involved.

**4. Classify the defects by type.** Different causes tend to leave different signatures:

| Defect type | Usually suggests |
|---|---|
| Silver streaks or splay, bubbles, brittleness | Moisture in the resin (humidity or drying) |
| Black specks, contamination, colour variation | The resin itself |
| Short shots, flash, sink marks, sticking in the mould | Process settings or how machines are operated, which can point to crew |

## Check how the resins interact with humidity

If you mould a resin that absorbs moisture, such as nylon, polycarbonate, PET or ABS, humidity and the resin can combine. The new supplier's resin might arrive with more moisture or absorb it faster. In that case, your existing drying times would no longer be enough in summer. Testing moisture content on incoming lots and after drying would show this. If it's the cause, the fix is longer drying, not a new supplier.

## A direct test before cancelling anything

If you have any of the old resin left, or can get a small quantity, run it and the new resin on the **same machine, same shift and same days**. Then compare defect rates. That separates the resin from the crew and the weather in a way that observational data can't.

## Bottom line

Cancelling a supply contract is costly and hard to reverse. Retraining a crew on a hunch also has costs, and may leave the real cause in place. The shift split and the defect types will probably narrow things down within a day or two, using data you already collect. Do those first, then decide.
